transcript:
Header: 2025-07-01 10:00 AM PST — Duration 45m — Recording: Zoom
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Connor Lee (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Nimbus Lead ML), Jon Ruiz (Nimbus Platform), Sara Kim (Nimbus Product)

[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check — same agenda as last week: review cache hit rates, look at the prompt reuse patterns, and decide tuning for TTLs and keying heuristics.
[00:12] Maya: Yep, sounds good. We ran the bench yesterday, I pulled some numbers into the sheet.
[00:20] Connor: Cool, did you include both prefix and KV cache metrics?
[00:24] Maya: Yeah, prefix and kv — though the export from our infra munged a couple of headers so some names are off.
[00:30] Jon: Sorry if my audio cuts, I'm on a hotspot, but I can jump in on infra stuff.
[00:35] Ava: No worries. Connor, can you take us through the Redwood telemetry we sent?
[00:40] Connor: Sure. So summary: across the 2-day run, canonical flow (catalog search + personalization) saw average prefix cache hit rate of 68% and KV cache hit of 54% for the session-windowed keys. Latency p50 for that flow was 210ms, p95 480ms — those are with current caching enabled.
[01:02] Maya: The 68% prefix hit — is that across all users or top 20% traffic? Because our reuse is very skewed.
[01:08] Connor: It's aggregated. If we filter by high-repeat users the prefix hit goes up to ~82%. For low-repeat or cold-start flows it's down to 35-40%.
[01:20] Sara: That matches what we see on product — VIP shoppers show repeated prompt prefixes (search context + user profile), but new visitors don't.
[01:28] Ava: Right. So the lever is twofold: keying heuristics to maximize reuse for the repeat flows, and TTL/bucket policies to avoid polluting cache with low-reuse prefixes.
[01:38] Jon: Can you explain the current keying? We hashed full prompt+session id right?
[01:43] Connor: Current production POC key is conversation_id + model_version + full_message_prefix. Problem is full prefix contains a lot of noise — timestamps, ephemeral tokens — so similar prefixes miss.
[01:55] Maya: We've seen 1:1 near-duplicates produce different keys because of tiny formatting changes.
[01:59] Connor: Exactly. So proposed change: normalize prefix (strip timestamps, canonicalize whitespace, remove ephemeral tokens), and then apply a short fingerprint on canonicalized prefix. Also add a user-segmentation bucket (high-frequency vs low) so we can use longer TTL for high-frequency bucket.
[02:18] Ava: TTL discussion — current TTL is 1 hour. For high-reuse flows we think 2-4 hours might be safe. For low-reuse, 15-30 minutes to avoid stale/large cache. Thoughts?
[02:29] Maya: 2 hours sounds reasonable for VIP flows. Our privacy compliance folks ok with that?
[02:34] Jon: From platform side, longer TTL increases memory pressure. But we can do per-pool limits and LRU eviction. Also we can pin hot keys on dedicated pool for the pilot.
[02:46] Connor: Right — Redwood Dedicated pool supports per-key pinning and we can cap memory per-model. For hosted, we recommend aggressive hashing + short TTL for tail.
[02:54] Ava: Quick question on KV cache semantics — are we seeing cross-turn reuse (KV reused across prompts in same session)?
[02:59] Maya: Yes, KV reuse within session is ~70% for our long sessions (3+ turns), but for typical 1-2 turn sessions reuse drops.
[03:09] Connor: So another lever — maintain a small per-session KV with a sliding window so we don't keep stale kvs for sessions that ended. That reduces memory while keeping reuse high for active sessions.
[03:19] Sara: Any risk to output quality with longer prefix caching? We worried about stale personalization effects.
[03:24] Connor: Good point. We plan to add validation hooks: flag keys that cross user-profile changes (e.g., updated cart) and invalidate. Also store a short profile checksum in the key so when profile changes, key misses.
[03:36] Maya: That checksum idea looks good. How much engineering lift to add the checksum?
[03:40] Connor: Small — it's just a 32-bit hash of the profile fields we care about. We can provide a snippet.
[03:45] Ava: Action: Connor will share instrumentation script and example cache-config JSON.
[03:50] [03:51] Jon: On the bench numbers — can we go over token savings? What percent of tokens did caching reduce?
[03:56] Connor: For the canonical flow, observed ~28% token reduction end-to-end. For high-repeat subset, token reduction up to 45%. That translates to roughly 20-30% cost savings for that route.
[04:09] Maya: Nice. Latency impact?
[04:11] Connor: p50 improved by ~35ms on average for cached requests, p95 improves more variably depending on KV perf. But some requests with cold cache are still heavy.
[04:21] Sara: We also saw occasional mis-attributions in the telemetry — some hits flagged as misses because of header mismatch. Could that be the cause of lower KV hit?
[04:29] Connor: Possibly — normalization fix should reduce that. Also we need consistent serialization, not ad-hoc JSON ordering.
[04:36] Maya: For prompt reuse strategy — we plan to move to canonical templates with slots for user-specific tokens, so the template becomes the cache key. That should massively improve prefix hits, right?
[04:45] Connor: Yes. If you can template out volatile parts and keep a stable template id, hit rates jump. But you need to manage template versioning (model_version + template_id).
[04:54] Ava: Example: instead of hashing full prompt with cart items inline, we use template "search_recommend_v1" + hash(cart_summary) in KV.
[05:02] Maya: We'll prototype two approaches: template-id keying and canonicalized-full text fingerprinting, and compare.
[05:08] Jon: For benchmarking, we need instrumentation on both client and server. Connor, can you provide the instrumentation script and CSV format?
[05:13] Connor: Yes — I'll attach a small script that emits per-request: timestamp, route, template_id, key_hash, prefix_hit (bool), kv_hit (bool), latency_ms, tokens_saved. We'll share schema.
[05:25] Ava: Security/compliance ask — Jon, you wanted SOC2 docs and network diagram.
[05:29] Jon: Yes, for the pilot approval I need the network diagram and details on key management.
[05:33] Ava: I'll send links to SOC2 and the network diagram PDF, and Connor will add a note about KMS integration (customer-managed keys).
[05:40] Sara: Anything else on tradeoffs? We're balancing memory cost vs token savings. If we push TTL too long we may not see additional savings but will use more memory.
[05:49] Connor: We can simulate memory impact by projecting unique key cardinality from today's logs — I'll run that projection with 1h/2h/4h TTL.
[05:57] Maya: Great. Also can we do a small controlled rollout: enable aggressive caching for 10% of traffic (high-repeat bucket) and monitor quality/regressions?
[06:05] Ava: Yes — Redwood supports route-level rollout and canary by user-seg. We'll set 10% canary for two days and look at rouge rates, latencies, and token savings.
[06:15] Jon: Timeline — if Redwood sends config by 7/3 we can enable canary by 7/6 and run bench 7/7-7/8.
[06:22] Ava: Sounds good. Recap of next steps: share config, instrumentation, SOC2 + network diagram, and schedule bench review.
[06:30] Maya: Quick nit — sometimes transcripts call the KV cache "KV cash" in our logs, lol.
[06:34] Connor: Haha, yes we've seen that in transcribed alerts.
[06:37] Ava: Any final Qs?
[06:40] Sara: One ask — can we include a short sample of normalized key before you send config? We want to see the actual string used for hashing.
[06:47] Connor: Will do; include example: template:search_v1|profile_hash:0x3fa2|slot_hash:0x1ac4
[06:54] Ava: Great. Thanks everyone, we’ll reconvene after bench.
[06:58] [END]
